READING 6
STATISTICAL DISTRIBUTIONS FOR
FINANCIAL ASSET PRICES AND
RETURNS
MODULE 6.1: PROBABILITY DISTRIBUTIONS
AND EXPECTED VALUES
LOS 6.a: Calculate, interpret, and evaluate unconditional expected values
for mean, variance, and covariance.
A random variable is a variable with an uncertain outcome, also referred to as a
stochastic variable. If the number of possible outcomes is countable, the
variable is referred to as a discrete random variable. An example of a discrete
random variable is the number of days it will rain in a month, because the
possible outcomes are countable, ranging from zero to the number of days in the
month. A random variable that has an infinite number of possible outcomes, such
as the monthly percentage change in a stock index, is referred to as a continuous
random variable.
A probability distribution describes the probabilities of all the possible
outcomes for a random variable. The probabilities of all possible outcomes must
sum to 1. A simple discrete probability distribution is the outcome of the roll of
one fair die. This has six possible outcomes, and each has a probability of one-
sixth, so their probabilities sum to 1.
A probability function, denoted p(x), specifies the probability that a random
variable is equal to a specific value. More formally, p(x) is the probability that
random variable X takes on the value x, or p(x) = P(X = x). We refer to a
probability function for a discrete random variable as a probability mass
function (PMF), and to a probability function for a continuous random variable
as a probability density function (PDF).

A probability function has two key properties:
Each outcome has a probability between zero and one inclusive, or 0 ≤ p(x) ≤ 1.
The sum of the probabilities for all possible outcomes equals 1, or ∑p(x) = 1.
EXAMPLE: Evaluating a probability function
Consider the following function: 
Determine whether this function satisfies the conditions for a probability
function.
Answer:
All the probabilities (1/10, 2/10, 3/10, and 4/10) are between 0 and 1, and the
sum of all the probabilities (1/10 + 2/10 + 3/10 + 4/10) equals 1, so both
conditions for a probability function are satisfied.
For a discrete distribution, p(x) = 0 when x cannot occur, or p(x) > 0 if it can.
Recall that p(x) is read as “the probability that random variable X = x.” For
example, the probability of it raining on 33 days in June is zero because June has
only 30 days, but the probability of it raining on 25 days in June has some
positive value.
For a continuous distribution, p(x) = 0, even though x can be the outcome,
because the number of possible outcomes is infinite. We can only meaningfully
consider the probability that an outcome will fall within a range, or P(x1 ≤ X ≤
x2), where x1 and x2 are actual numbers. For example, the probability of
receiving exactly two inches of rain in June is effectively zero, because two
inches is a single point in an infinite range of possible values. However, the
probability of the amount of rain being between 1.99 and 2.01 inches has some
positive value. In the case of continuous distributions, P(x1 ≤ X ≤ x2) is equal to
P(x1 < X < x2), because p(x1) = p(x2) = 0.
In finance, we treat some discrete distributions as though they are continuous
because the number of possible outcomes is very large. For example, the
increase or decrease in the price of a stock traded on an American exchange is
recorded in dollars and cents. Analysts generally do not believe their pricing
models are precise enough to assign a probability to an outcome such as a
change of exactly $1.47. It is customary, therefore, to speak in terms of the
probability of a range of possible price changes—say, between $1.00 and $2.00.

A cumulative distribution function (CDF), or simply distribution function,
defines the probability that a random variable X takes on a value less than or
equal to a specific value, x. It represents the sum, or cumulative value, of the
probabilities for the outcomes up to and including a specified outcome. The CDF
for a random variable, X, may be expressed as F(x) = P(X ≤ x).
Consider the probability function we defined in our earlier example, X = {1, 2,
3, 4}, p(x) = x / 10. For this distribution, F(3) = 0.1 + 0.2 + 0.3 = 0.6, and F(4) =
0.1 + 0.2 + 0.3 + 0.4 = 1. This means that F(3) is the cumulative probability that
outcomes 1, 2, or 3 occur, and F(4) is the cumulative probability that one of the
four possible outcomes occurs.
Figure 6.1 shows an example of a CDF (for a standard normal distribution,
which we will describe later in this reading). It has a 15.87% probability of a
value less than −1. This is the total area to the left of −1 in the PDF in Panel (a),
and the y-axis value of the CDF for a value of −1 in Panel (b).
Figure 6.1: Standard Normal Probability Density and Cumulative Distribution
Functions

EXAMPLE: Cumulative distribution function
Cermak Company’s return on equity is a continuous distribution over the range
from −20% to +30% and has a CDF of F(x) = (x + 20) / 50. Calculate the
probability that its return on equity will be between 0% and 15%.
Answer:
To determine the probability of an outcome between 0% and 15%, we can first
calculate the probability that return on equity will be less than or equal to 15%,
or F(15), and then from that, subtract the probability that ROE will be less than
zero, or F(0):
P(0 ≤ x ≤ 15) = F(15) − F(0)
F(15) = (15 + 20) / 50 = 0.70
F(0) = (0 + 20) / 50 = 0.40
F(15) − F(0) = 0.70 − 0.40 = 0.30 = 30%

probability-weighted average of a random variable’s possible outcomes. For a
discrete random variable X, where xi is a possible value of X and P(xi) is its
probability, we can express the expected value as follows:

An unconditional variance is the squared spread of a random variable around
its expected value, and an unconditional standard deviation is the square root
of unconditional variance:

MODULE 6.2: DISCRETE AND CONTINUOUS
PROBABILITY DISTRIBUTIONS
LOS 6.b: Calculate, interpret, and evaluate the principal moments of key
statistical distributions used in finance.
PROFESSOR’S NOTE
We do not believe candidates are (or should be) required to memorize or
dive deeply into the formulas for the principal moments of all these
distributions. While we reproduce these formulas for reference, our text
describing the individual distributions will indicate those features and
moments we think are important for understanding their characteristics.

Discrete Distributions
Figure 6.2 lists the mathematical expressions for the four key moments of three
kinds of discrete distributions: a discrete uniform distribution, a binomial
distribution, and a Poisson distribution.
Figure 6.2: Moments for Discrete Statistical Distributions
Discrete Uniform Distribution
A discrete uniform distribution is one for which the probabilities for all
possible outcomes are equal. It has n possible outcomes ranging from a to b, and
the probability of each outcome is 1 / n.
For example, consider a discrete uniform probability distribution defined as X =
{1, 2, 3, 4, 5}, p(x) = 0.2. The expected value of X is (a + b) / 2 = 3, which is
also the mean of the equally likely possible outcomes.
The variance of a discrete uniform distribution is given by:
For the discrete uniform distribution X = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}, the variance equals:
The CDF for the nth outcome, F(xn), is np(x). The probability for a range of
outcomes is kp(x), where k is the number of possible outcomes in the range.
Figure 6.3 illustrates the CDF for this discrete uniform variable.
Figure 6.3: Probability and CDFs

Binomial Distribution
A binomial distribution is also a discrete distribution. The random variable is
the number of “successes” from a given number of trials, for which the outcome
of each trial can be either “success” or “failure.” The probability of success, p, is
constant for each trial, and the trials are independent (i.e., success or failure in
the next trial is not affected by the outcomes of previous trials). A binomial
random variable for which the number of trials is 1 is called a Bernoulli
distribution.
For a given series of n trials, the expected number of successes, or E(X), is given
by this formula:
E(X) = np
The intuition is straightforward. If we perform n trials and the probability of
success on each trial is p, we expect np successes.
The variance of a binomial random variable is given by this formula:

variance of X = np(1 − p)
EXAMPLE: Expected value of a binomial random variable
Based on empirical data, an analyst estimates that the probability of the Dow
Jones Industrial Average (DJIA) increasing on any given day is 0.67.
Assuming the only other outcome is that it decreases, we can state p(Up) =
0.67 and p(Down) = 0.33. Further, assume that movements in the DJIA are
independent (i.e., an increase in one day is independent of what happened on
another day).
Calculate the expected value and the variance of the number of up days in a
five-day period.
Answer:
Using binomial terminology, we define success as Up, so p = 0.67:
E(X | n = 5, p = 0.67) = (5)(0.67) = 3.35
Because the binomial distribution is a discrete distribution, the result X = 3.35
is not a possible outcome. However, if we were to record the results of many
five-day periods, the average number of up days (successes) would converge to
3.35 as the number of 5-day periods gets large.
The variance of the random variable is 5(0.67)(1 − 0.67) = 1.1055
Binomial random variables can be used to model possible stock prices over
multiple periods. In the binomial model, the price of the stock can move up or
down at each time step. The stock price at each node is calculated as follows:

factor of 1.02 and a monthly down factor of 1 / 1.02 = 0.9804. The stock’s
price today is $10.00. According to this model, what will the stock price be
after two up months and three down months?
Answer:
We can illustrate a binomial model with a probability tree or decision tree.
Figure 6.4 shows a probability tree for the stock price model in our previous
example. Because this model defined the up factor and the down factor as
reciprocals, an up move followed by a down move or a down move followed by
an up move results in no change in the price—and two up moves and three down
moves result in a price of $9.80, regardless of the order in which the moves
occur.
In our example, we did not assign probabilities to the price paths. An analyst can
design a binomial model to exhibit various probability functions by choosing
different probabilities of success.
Figure 6.4: Probability Tree
Poisson Distribution
The Poisson distribution is often used to model the number of times a specific
event is expected to occur within a given interval of time. It is assumed that the
events happen independently at a known constant rate, which we denote as λ.
The probability of observing k events in a time interval t is stated as follows:

For a single unit of time (t = 1), the mean and variance of a Poisson distribution
are both equal to λ. It has skewness of 
 and excess kurtosis of 
Analysts use the Poisson distribution to model how frequently a rare event can
be expected to occur. The Poisson distribution can be thought of as the
mathematical limit of the binomial distribution, as the number of trials n
approaches infinity and the probability p of an event approaches zero.

A portfolio contains 800 bonds. The probability of any single bond defaulting
within one year is 0.5%. Calculate (1) the probability of a default occurring
within one year, and (2) the probability of exactly three bonds defaulting
within a year.
Answer:

Continuous Distributions
Figure 6.5 lists the mathematical expressions for the key moments of four kinds
of continuous distributions: a continuous uniform distribution, a normal
distribution, a log-normal distribution, and a logistic distribution.
Figure 6.5: Moments for Continuous Statistical Distributions
Continuous Uniform Distribution
A continuous uniform distribution is defined over a range that spans between
some lower limit, a, and some upper limit, b. Outcomes can only occur between
a and b, and because the distribution is continuous, even within the range from a
to b, the probability of any single outcome is zero. We can only speak
meaningfully of the probability that an outcome will fall within a range.

Formally, the probability of outcomes between x1 and x2 (assuming x1 and x2 fall
between the boundaries a and b) equals 
Do not miss how simple this is just because the notation is mathematical. For a
continuous uniform distribution, the probability of outcomes in a range that is
one-half the whole range is 50%. The probability of outcomes in a range that is
one-quarter of the possible range is 25%.
EXAMPLE: Continuous uniform distribution
X is uniformly distributed between 2 and 12. Calculate the probability that X
will be between 4 and 8.
Answer:
Figure 6.6 illustrates this continuous uniform distribution. Note that the area
bounded by 4 and 8 is 40% of the total probability between 2 and 12 (which is
100%).
Figure 6.6: Continuous Uniform Distribution
Because outcomes are equal over equal-size possible intervals, the CDF is
linear over the variable’s range. The CDF for the distribution in the example,
Prob (X < x), is shown in Figure 6.7.
Figure 6.7: CDF for a Continuous Uniform Variable

The mean of a continuous uniform distribution is its midpoint, 
 Its
variance, 
 is proportional to the squared width of the interval from a to b.
Its skew is zero (the distribution is symmetric), and its kurtosis is 1.8 (therefore,
excess kurtosis is 1.8 − 3 = −1.2).
Uniform distributions are used for large-scale Monte Carlo simulation, a
computational method that uses repeated random sampling to produce a
distribution of the outcomes from a complex process, such as the value of an
option based on multiple stochastic inputs. We can then use the distribution of
simulated outcomes to calculate the expected value of the option as the mean of
the many outcomes, and the expected variance of the option value as the
variance of the many outcomes.
PROFESSOR’S NOTE
We will discuss Monte Carlo simulation in our reading on the
simulation of financial asset prices and returns.
Normal Distribution
The well-known normal distribution (also known as a Gaussian distribution)
is a symmetrical, bell-shaped curve. The bell shape indicates that outcomes are
more likely to occur closer to the mean.
A normal distribution is defined completely by its mean and standard deviation,
expressed as N(μ,σ), because its skewness is zero and its excess kurtosis is zero
(i.e., it exhibits kurtosis of 3).
The normal distribution is important for many reasons. Many of the random
variables that are relevant to finance and other professional disciplines follow a

normal distribution. In the area of investment and portfolio management, the
normal distribution plays a central role in portfolio theory.
Many independent random variables, or sums of them, tend toward a normal
distribution, even if the original variables themselves are not normally
distributed. Binomial distributions converge to normal distributions as the
number of trials, n, gets large.
A normal distribution with a mean of zero and a variance (and standard
deviation) of 1, or N(0,1), is termed a standard normal distribution. Figure 6.8
illustrates the PDF and CDF of a standard normal distribution, where the
horizontal axes represent numbers of standard deviations from the mean.
Figure 6.8: Standard Normal Distribution1
In subsequent readings in statistical analysis, we will use two facts about a
normal distribution to draw statistical inferences:
Approximately 68% of the outcomes are within one standard deviation of its
mean.
Approximately 95% of the outcomes are within two standard deviations of its
mean.
Log-Normal Distribution
A log-normal distribution is used to model data where only positive values can
occur, and observations may differ by several degrees of magnitude. It is the
probability distribution of a random variable where the natural logarithm (ln) of
the variable is normally distributed.

A log-normal distribution has outcomes equal to ex, where x follows a normal
distribution and e is the base of the natural logarithm—a constant approximately
equal to 2.7183.
Because the value ex cannot be negative (e to the power negative infinity is
zero), a log-normal variable cannot produce outcomes less than zero. This makes
a log-normal distribution well suited to model asset prices, which do not take on
negative values. The positive values are not bounded, so the right-hand tail is
long, and the distribution is right-skewed. Figure 6.9 illustrates these
characteristics for three log-normal distributions.
Figure 6.9: Log-Normal Distributions2
PROFESSOR’S NOTE
A log-normal distribution is described by two parameters, mean and
standard deviation, referred to as the location parameter and scale
parameter. This is not the standard deviation of the x variable, but the
standard deviation of the variable once it has been transformed into a
normal distribution—in other words, ln(x). In Figure 6.9, the location
parameter and scale parameter are given by m and s, respectively.
The mean and variance of a log-normal random variable Y, where Y = eX, are
expressed mathematically as follows:

with the advantage that they will not create negative stock prices. The “drift

Assume a stock’s price follows a log-normal distribution, has a price today of
£10, and has a mean logarithmic annual return of 6% with a standard deviation
of 12%. Calculate the expected stock price in three years.
Answer:
Logistic Distribution
Another distribution that is useful for financial analysis is the logistic
distribution. A logistic distribution resembles a normal distribution in shape, but
it has fatter tails. Like the normal distribution, the logistic distribution is centered
on its mean. A logistic distribution has a scale parameter s, that affects only its
variance, which equals 
A logistic distribution is bell-shaped and symmetric like a normal distribution, so
its skew is zero. Because it has fatter tails than a normal distribution, it has
positive excess kurtosis, which is equal to 1.2.
In financial analysis, the logistic distribution is employed in logistic regression,
in which the predicted (dependent) variable is binary (often 0 and 1, for “will not
happen” and “will happen”) and is determined by one or more independent

variables. The logistic distribution is also used in machine learning and AI
applications.

MODULE 6.3: CONDITIONAL EXPECTATIONS
AND BAYESIAN UPDATING
LOS 6.c: Calculate, interpret, and evaluate conditional expectations,
variances, and covariances.
A joint probability distribution describes the probabilities for multiple
variables and, importantly, how they vary over time relative to each other. A
bivariate distribution is for two variables; it requires information on their

means and variances and how they are distributed relative to each other, by
either their covariance or their correlation.
Specifically, a joint bivariate CDF, F12(x1, x2), quantifies the joint probability of
outcomes in which the random variable X1 does not exceed a value x1, and the
random variable X2 does not exceed a value x2. Formally, we can describe a joint
CDF for the two variables as:
Figure 6.10 illustrates such a joint probability function where the height of the
plot is the probability of joint outcomes of X1 and X2. For continuous random
variables, the height is proportional to the probability in a small range of
outcomes around the specific values of X1 and X2.
Figure 6.10: Joint PDF3
For discrete random variables, instead of using a three-dimensional graph, we
can represent a joint probability distribution with a contingency table that
summarizes their relationship with the frequencies at which certain combinations
of the random variables occur. Figure 6.11 illustrates such a table for the stocks
in an index, with ranges of returns outcomes for two categories of firms.
Figure 6.11: Contingency Table for Discrete Variables

The sums in the bottom row are the marginal distributions by firm type, and
those in the right-most column are marginal distributions by rate of return. The
probability that a randomly selected firm in the index is a financial firm is 300 /
500 = 60%. The probability that a firm in the index will have returns less than or
equal to 8% is 240 / 500 = 48%. The probability that a randomly selected firm is
nonfinancial and has returns greater than 8% is 140 / 500 = 28%.
A conditional mean is the expected value of a random variable given that a
certain condition is true. In general, we can express this for random variable X as
E(X|S), which we read as the expected value of X given that the condition S is
met.
For a discrete random variable X, the conditional mean is the sum of the possible
values of X times their conditional probabilities.
The conditional variance measures the variation of a random variable around
its conditional mean:
The conditional covariance measures how two variables move together if a
condition S is met:

LOS 6.d: Formulate investment problems through Bayesian updating.
Bayes’ formula is used to update a prior probability, or a priori probability,
of a given event for new information. The updated probability is referred to as a
posterior probability. We can derive Bayes’ formula using the multiplication
rule for conditional probability.
The multiplication rule is that P(B|A) × P(A) = P(BA). That is, the conditional
probability of B occurring given A, times the unconditional probability that A
will occur, equals the unconditional probability that both B and A will occur. By
the same logic, we can also state that P(A|B) × P(B) = P(AB).
We also know that the joint probability of A and B occurring is the same as the
joint probability of B and A occurring: P(BA) = P(AB).
From these facts, we can write P(A|B) P(B) = P(B|A) P(A), as both sides of the
equation are equal to the joint probability that A and B will both occur.
Bayes’ formula is derived by dividing both sides of this equality by the
unconditional probability P(B):
EXAMPLE: Bayes’ formula

There is a 60% probability that the economy will outperform—and if it does,
there is a 70% probability a stock will have gains and a 30% probability the
stock will have no gains. There is a 40% probability the economy will
underperform, and if it does, there is a 20% probability the stock in question
will have gains and an 80% probability it will not. Given that the stock has
gained, calculate the updated probability that the economy outperformed.
Answer:
In the figure just presented, we have multiplied the probabilities to calculate
the probabilities of each of the four outcome pairs. Note that these sum to 1.
Given that the stock has gains, what is our updated probability of an
outperforming economy? We sum the probability of stock gains in both states
(outperform and underperform) to get 42% + 8% = 50%, which is the
unconditional probability of gains. Given that the stock has gains and using
Bayes’ formula, the probability that the economy has outperformed is 
 Given that the stock has gained in value, the market will have
outperformed 84% of the time—which is our updated (posterior) probability
that the economy will have outperformed after learning that the stock has
gains.

KEY CONCEPTS
LOS 6.a
A discrete random variable has a countable number of possible outcomes. A
continuous random variable has an infinite number of possible outcomes within
a defined range.
The probability density function for continuous variables is proportional to the
probability of outcomes in an interval around a given value.
A cumulative distribution function, or simply distribution function, defines the
probability that a random variable takes on a value equal to or less than a
specific value.
The unconditional expected value of a random variable is the weighted average
of its possible outcomes:
Unconditional variance is the probability-weighted sum of the squared
deviations from the mean or expected value. The unconditional standard

deviation is the positive square root of the unconditional variance.
LOS 6.b
The four principal moments of a distribution are its mean, variance, skew, and
kurtosis.
Distributions commonly used in finance are the discrete uniform, binomial,
continuous uniform, Poisson, normal, log-normal, and logistic:
A discrete uniform distribution is one for which the probabilities for all
possible outcomes are equal.
A binomial distribution has two possible outcomes and can be used to model
asset prices over multiple periods.
A continuous uniform distribution is used to generate random outcomes, such
as those used in Monte Carlo simulations.
A Poisson distribution models the number of times an event occurs over a
specified time period.
A normal distribution is completely described by its mean and variance and is
often used for hypothesis testing and statistical inference.
A log-normal distribution is bounded from below by zero, which makes it
suitable for modeling asset prices over time.
A logistic distribution is employed in regression models with a binary
dependent variable and is used in machine learning and AI.
LOS 6.c
The joint density of two random variables describes the probability distribution
of all possible pairs of outcomes.
A conditional distribution is the distribution of a random variable, given a
restriction on the values of other variables in a joint probability distribution.
Conditional expectations represent the expected value of a random variable
under certain conditions using the appropriate conditional distribution.
Probability trees illustrate the probabilities of possible outcomes over multiple
periods.
LOS 6.d
